modules.subtitle: A note from Dr. Geoff Angell, DPT
modules.body:
![IMG-15: Picture of the author in a lab coat or scrubs with company logo. Could be standing or sitting on edge of desk/treatment table.]()

**Welcome to the Fall Prevention Plan,** I am Dr. Geoff Angell, DPT, the author, and a physical therapist that specializes in the treatment of balance disorders and falls in older adults.

If I've learned anything in my 21 + year career as a physical therapist, it is that **falls are a major concern for senior. They are common, frequently hazardous, and often catastrophic life changing events.** Despite their prevalence and potential severity, **falls don’t have to be such a big problem. Effective and easy-to-implement strategies exist that can dramatically reduce their risk.**

Unfortunately, until now there hasn't been a single resource that presented a comprehensive strategy to reduce the risk of falls and then thoroughly explained how to implement it. **The Fall Prevention Plan was created for this purpose. It provides an easy to follow and complete plan to decrease the risk of falls** that blends proven fall prevention techniques with the clinical experience of a physical therapist that has provided over 10,000 successful balance and fall prevention treatments.

### The Fall Prevention Plan consists of a 5 BASIC PARTS:

- A brief overview of balance and falls
- The 10 Point Fall Prevention Plan
- The "If a Fall Occurs" Strategy
- A Mobility Equipment Appendix to help you select the right assistive device
- A Home Modification and Equipment Appendix to make your home safe.

**For MORE PERSONALIZED SUPPORT, the Fall Prevention Plan also provides video access to:**

- Professionally lead Balance Exercise Classes
- Monthly Fall Prevention Topic Discussion with author Q&A
- One on One Consultation services

![IMG-16: ***picture signifying hope —> older couple walking in the distance with a beautiful scenery behind them or playing with grandchildren.]()

**The Fall Prevention Plan is a proven fall reduction solution.** It can have a profound effect on the lives of all who use it, empowering them to live life to the fullest. It is my sincere hope that The Fall Prevention Plan will help you too.

modules.title: Introduction
modules.subtitle: Section 1
modules.body:
![IMG-17: picture of an older adult lying face down on the ground after a fall.]()

**Falling is one of the greatest risks faced by older adults today.** They can lead to diminished balance confidence, decreased participation in daily activity, nursing home placement, serious injury and even death.
---
![IMG-18: Picture of an ambulance in front of a home responding to an emergency.]()

**Sadly, falls are alarmingly common and frequently hazardous**— CDC statistics show that they are the leading cause of injury and injury-related death among seniors in the United States, with roughly 14 million falls, over 5 million injuries, and 34,000 deaths reported annually.
---
![IMG-19: Picture of a son/daughter and older parent, heads together, grieving or faces showing worry.]()

Needless to say, falling is a very serious problem and these statistics could make one question if anything **can actually be done to prevent them?**
---
![IMG-20: Picture of an older adult couple enjoying themselves/being happy, while engaging in an outdoor activity.]()

**Fortunately, the answer is a resounding YES! Falls are treatable.** They don't have to be an inevitable part of aging. Research shows that most falls are preventable and fall risk can be significantly reduced.
---
![IMG-21: Picture of an older adult exercising or walking with a cane or walking, being happy and looking purposeful.]()

**How is this accomplished?** Studies indicate that implementing a multifaceted strategy combining targeted fall-prevention techniques, balance focused strengthening exercises, and a well-designed balance program is the most effective way to prevent falls.

![IMG-22: Picture of  a happy family setting showing older adults with walkers or canes; surroundings are peaceful/hopeful.]()

**The Fall Prevention Plan was created for this purpose. It is the answer to increased fall risk. It is a simple, but thorough guide to create a personalized fall prevention strategy** that incorporates targeted fall reduction techniques, strengthening exercises, and a personalized balance program. This plan is your roadmap to a safer life. It empowers you to significantly lower your chance of falling by helping to pinpoint key risk factors and then outlining the most effective strategies to address them.
---
**To make the most of the program, review each section carefully, reflecting on how the recommendations apply to you, and then commit to integrating them into your daily routine. By doing so, you can enjoy a safer, more confident, and independent life!**

modules.title: An Overview of Balance and Falls
modules.subtitle: Section 2
modules.body:
**Before starting the journey to reduce fall risk, it's important to have a basic understanding of balance and falls — what they are, how balance is created, and what causes falls to occur. Let's look at this now.**
---
### What is a Fall?

![IMG-23: Picture of someone on the ground after a fall.]()

**A fall is an unexpected event where the body comes to rest on the ground**, with or without injury.
---
![IMG-24: Picture of someone balancing, like on a tightrope or a rock in the middle of the river, or standing on one leg.]()

### What is Balance?

**Balance is the act of maintaining physical stability** and the body's primary defense against falling.
---
### How is Balance Created?

![IMG-25: Pictures illustrate the Sequence of physiologic events needed to]()

**Balance is created through a complex sequence of events involving multiple body systems working together to create a stable body position.** The process is automatic, subconscious, almost instantaneous, and looks something like this:

The body's sensory systems gather data about its position and movement relative to the surrounding environment. This information is sent to the brain and spinal cord where it is analyzed and a plan to maintain balance is created. The newly formulated instructions are then sent to the muscles to carry out the movements needed to maintain a stable body position and avoid falling.
---
![IMG-26: Picture of someone tripping/slipping, maybe on a banana peel.]()

### What Causes Falls?

**Falls happen when the body becomes unsteady and any attempt it makes to regain a balanced position fails.**

modules.title: Performing a Fall Risk Assessment
modules.subtitle: Section 3
modules.body:
**Now that you have a basic understanding of balance and falls, you are in a good position to perform a Fall Risk Assessment to identify the specific factors that increase your risk of falling and then determine how likely you are to fall.**
---
### Identifying Your Fall Risk Factors

**The first step in performing a Fall Risk Assessment is to identify anything that could increase your risk of falling.**

![IMG-27: Picture of Sherlock Holmes type figure with magnifying glass or just a magnifying glass.]()

**There are many factors that cause the body to become unsteady and fall, but understanding specifically what triggers your own unsteadiness is key to improving your safety.** This knowledge pinpoints the most likely reason you might fall and therefore begins to create the framework for an effective Fall Prevention Plan.
---
**Below is a list of the most common causes of falls. Review it and try to determine which are most likely to affect you.**

### The Most Common Causes of Falls

- Muscle or joint stiffness
- Poor endurance
- Muscle weakness
- Reduced sensation
- Poor balance
- Dizziness
- Altered posture
- Low vision
- Pain
- Excessive weight
- Impulsive movements
- Abnormal walking patterns
- Decreased cognition
- Limited safety awareness
- Low acceptance of disability
- Reduced short-term memory
- Incontinence
- Polypharmacy (multiple medications)
- Adverse medication side effects
- Poor fluid intake
- Inadequate nutrition
- Poorly fitting footwear
- Improperly prescribed or fitted mobility devices
- Assistive device non-use
- Cluttered home environment
- Poor lighting
- Unsafe/unlevel terrain
- Lack of appropriate medical equipment in high-risk areas (e.g., shower, toilet)

### What did recognize that could increase your risk of falling?

*The fall risk factor tool could list the causes of falls the member has indicated***
---
### Quantifying Your Fall Risk

**The second step in performing a Fall Risk Assessment is to quantify your fall risk.**

![IMG-28: Picture of tools that can measure: scale, calculator, tape measure]()

**Determining how likely you are to fall is also very important to understand when creating a Fall Prevention Plan** as it helps select the strategies that will be most effective in reducing your chance of falling.
---
**One tool that can be used to determine how likely your are to fall is the Timed Up and Go Test, or TUG Test.**

### To perform the TUG Test:

- Place a sturdy chair in an open area.
- Mark a line ten feet from the chair.
- Time yourself as you stand, walk to the line at a normal pace, turn, walk back, and sit down.
---
### To make an estimate of Fall Risk using the TUG TEST:

- Compare the time it took to complete the TUG Test to the following standard data to estimate fall risk:

| Time to Complete Test=Fall Risk |
|---|
| Less than 10 seconds          = Low fall risk |
| 10-14.9 seconds  =           Moderate fall risk |
| Greater than 15 seconds    = High fall risk |

---
### Here's a short video showing how to perform the TUG Test:

[video:V1 Video of the TUG Test being performed.]()
---

### How did you do?

modules.title: Creating a Fall Prevention Plan
modules.subtitle: Chapter 2
modules.body:
![IMG-30: Picture of a clipboard w/ the word fall prevention plan on it and checkmarks next to illegible writing.]()

**Now that you have a basic understanding of balance and falls, have identified the factors that increase your risk of falling, and determined how likely you are to fall, you're ready to tackle the problem of increased fall risk by creating a personalized Fall Prevention Plan.** To do this, you will be introduced to the 10 most common areas related to falls and the best strategies known to prevent them.

### The Topics to be discussed include:

- Mindset
- Footwear
- Vision
- Medication
- Nutrition and Hydration
- Posture
- Home Safety
- Assistive Device Selection
- Strength
- Balance

**As you explore these sections, take the time needed to understand each problem area and their suggested solutions. Then determine the fall prevention strategies that would help you the most and begin working to incorporate them into your daily routine.** The Fall Prevention Plan isn't a one-time task, instead it's a guide for a safety-focused lifestyle. Stay consistent with its recommendations and you'll significantly reduce your risk of falls!

modules.title: Mindset
modules.subtitle: Step 1
modules.body:
**The first step in the Fall Prevention Plan is adopting a safety-first mindset.**

![IMG-31: Picture of someone thinking, coming up with a great idea or determing that they are going to do something]()

**Choosing to be safe, that is making a conscious decision to prioritize not falling, is key to preventing falls and the foundation of an effective Fall Prevention Plan.**

### How do you accomplish this?

1. Acknowledge your increased fall risk. 2. Stay alert to factors that could worsen your risk of falling.
3. Commit to using strategies that lower your chances of falling.

modules.title: Footwear
modules.subtitle: Step 2
modules.body:
**The second step in the Fall Prevention Plan is choosing the right footwear.**
---
![IMG-32: Picture of a shoes with good features]()

**Proper shoes play a key role in reducing fall risk and should be selected with that goal in mind.** Shoes should enhance balance and minimize the chance of falling.

Brand doesn't matter, instead find shoes that are comfortable, fit properly, have good arch support, a flat or low-pitched soul, a closed heel, a non-aggressive tread, and if able, the ability to be fastened securely.

---
![IMG-33: Picture of bad shoes]()

Stay away from high heels, slip on shoes without a closed heel, sandals without a back strap, or running shoes.
---
### To Reduce Fall Risk, Use One of the Following Shoe Styles:

![IMG-34: Walking shoe]()

- Walking shoe

![IMG-35: Slip on shoe]()

- Properly fitted slip-on shoe

![IMG-36: Lace up shoe]()

- Lace up dress shoe

![IMG-37: Sandal with fastening  strap at toe and heel]()

- Sandal with fastening

straps at the toe and heel

modules.title: Vision
modules.subtitle: Step 3
modules.body:
**The third step in the Fall Prevention Plan is properly managing your vision.**

![IMG-38: Picture of someone getting an eye exam or of eyeglasses or an eyechart]()

**Clear vision helps you navigate your surroundings and is therefore vital for maintaining balance.**
---
### To Reduce Fall Risk, Prioritize Eye Health with These 5 Steps:

1. Get regular eye exams.
2. Wear your prescribed eyewear.
3. Follow your doctor's advice on vision medications and treatments.
4. Acknowledge any visual impairments and adjust your routine or environment as needed (ensure adequate lighting throughout your home, don't walk outside or drive at night, and mark stair edges with contrasting tape, etc...).
5. If multifocal lens glasses (bifocals, trifocals, or progressives) cause your vision to be distorted, consider having multiple sets of glasses. One pair for distance vision needs and another pair for close-up tasks.

modules.title: Medication and Balance
modules.subtitle: Step 4
modules.body:
**The fourth step in the Fall Prevention Plan is properly managing your medications.**

![IMG-39: Picture of pill bottles/medication or a person speaking to a pharmacist.]()

**Medications are designed to improve health, but sadly some have negative side effects or interactions with other medications that increase the risk of falls.** This phenomenon occurs more frequently in the older adult population where taking multiple medications and slowed drug metabolism is common.
---
**To minimize your risk of falling due to a medication, following this action plan:**

1. Take all prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, vitamins, and supplements only as directed.
2. Keep an updated list of all prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, vitamins, and supplements, noting dosages and frequency taken.
3. Share this list with every doctor at each appointment.
4. Inform your primary care physician about any medication changes made by specialists.
5. Regularly review your medication list with your primary care physician and pharmacist to identify harmful interactions, duplicates, or unnecessary prescriptions.
6. Discuss fall risk concerns with your doctors and request that medications with minimal impact on balance be considered. If a medication increases fall risk and no alternatives exist, ask for strategies to reduce its effects.

[download:Medication List]()

### Keep Track of Your Medications with Our Downloadable Medication List

- Record medication name, dosage, frequency and amount taken, and prescribing provider.

modules.title: Nutrition and Hydration
modules.subtitle: Step 5
modules.body:
**The fifth step in the Fall Prevention Plan is consuming a diet that minimizes your chances of falling.**
---
![IMG-40: Picture of the Food Pyramid]()

**Maintaining proper nutrition and hydration plays a key role in reducing your risk of falls.** In fact, poor dietary intake is actually the leading cause of serious falls (those requiring hospital admission) for senior adults.
---
![IMG-41: Picture of a healthy senior engaging in activity]()

**A Diet that consists of the proper amount of calories and fluid will help to maximize your strength, mental clarity, balance, and fall avoidance.**
---
![IMG-42: Picture of frail/ less well looking senior having to use a walker or cane and having difficult with their mobility (stooped posture).]()

**While a diet lacking an adequate amount of calories and fluid can lead to weakness, confusion, unsteadiness, and ultimately increased fall risk.**
---

![IMG-43: Picture of a healthy, muscular older adult engaging in exercise.]()

**The types of nutrients your diet consists of is also a very important. A Diet rich in protein will** help create a lean body with higher levels of energy, greater amounts of muscle, and that is generally better able to manage unsteadiness and avoid falls.

![IMG-44: Picture of an overweight older adult needing an assistive device for mobility.]()

**Whereas, a diet rich in carbohydrates and sugar will** create a body with higher percentages of fat, lower amounts of energy, smaller amounts of muscle, and that is generally more susceptible to unsteadiness and falling.
---
**To minimize your chances of falling, maintaining a good diet is key.**

Below are the recommended dietary guidelines to help you take in the proper amount of calories, fluid, and protein:

### Recommended Daily Calorie Intake for Senior Adult Males:

| Activity Level | Calories Needed Per Day |
|---|---|
| Sedentary | 2,000-2,200 calories |
| Moderately Active | 2,200-2,400 calories |
| Highly Active | 2,400-2,800 calories |

### Recommended Daily Calorie Intake for Senior Adult Females:

| Activity Level | Calories Needed Per Day |
|---|---|
| Sedentary | 1,600 calories |
| Moderately Active | 1.800 calories |
| Highly Active | 2,000-2,200 calories |

### A Special Note on Protein:

**When it comes to fall prevention, protein is the super nutrient.**
---
![IMG-45: Picture of a muscular person or large bicep or a cartoon figure displaying protein as a superhero, standing with hands on hip, and cape flapping in wind.]()

**Protein serves a dual function of fueling the body to perform daily activities and as the building block muscle, one of the body's primary reducers of fall risk.** To maintain or build muscle, senior adults should aim to consume between 0.54 – 0.72 grams of protein per pound of body weight per day.
---
![IMG-46: Picture of the different Protein Sources]()

**The primary protein sources for the body are meat, poultry, fish, dairy, beans, lentils, nuts, and seeds.** Below is a list of common foods and their protein content to help you determine if your current diet is adequate.

modules.title: Creating a Safe Home Environment
modules.subtitle: Step 6
modules.body:
**The sixth step in the Fall Prevention Plan is to create a safe home environment.**
---
![IMG-54: Picture of a modest, but peaceful/warm/inviting home.]()

**Most falls happen in the comfort of one's own home.** Despite the majority of people feeling safest there, homes are actually the most likely place for falls to occur. Fortunately, there is a solution. Research shows that implementing simple home safety modifications can significantly reduce the chance of falling there.

---
### Here are proven ways to make your home safer:

- Keep your home clean and clutter-free.
- Arrange furniture to create clear and wide walking paths.
- Remove throw rugs or secure their edges to the floor.
- Organize closets and cabinets to avoid excessive reaching or bending.
- Ensure adequate lighting indoors and on outdoor walkways.
- Install nightlights in frequently used areas.
- Use chairs eighteen to twenty-two inches tall with backs and arms.
- In the bathroom, install a raised toilet seat with armrests, grab bars at the entrance of and in the tub or shower, and non-slip strips on the tub or shower floor. If your balance is moderate to significantly compromised, consider a shower chair with a back and arms. If stepping over the tub wall is difficult, consider using a tub bench.
- Set your bed height between eighteen to twenty-three inches (when sat on) and add a Bed Rail or Wonder Pole if getting in and out is challenging.
- Create a designated dressing area with a sturdy chair and solid surface for support.
- Ensure stairs are well-lit, have handrails on one or both sides, and feature marked edges for visibility.

**For a thorough explanation of home modifications and durable medical equipment that can be used to improve the safety of the home environment and assistance with ordering, please refer to the section titled Appendix of Home Safety Modifications and Equipment**.

modules.title: Choosing an Assistive Devices (Cane, Walker, Wheelchair)
modules.subtitle: Step 7
modules.body:
**The seventh step in the Fall Prevention Plan is selecting the appropriate assistive device.**
---
![IMG-55: Picture of 1-2 seniors confidently walking with a cane, walker, or both.]()

**Assistive devices are very effective for improving balance and safety, and are generally considered to be one of the best fall prevention strategies available.** They also boost strength, confidence, activity level, and overall quality of life and are therefore strongly recommended if a person has an increased risk of falls.

---
**There are four main types of assistive devices: Canes, 2 Wheel Rolling Walkers, 4 Wheel Rolling Walkers, and Wheelchairs.**

![IMG-56: Picture of a cane]()

![IMG-57: Picture of a 2 wheel rolling walker]()

![IMG-58: Picture of a 4 wheel rolling walker]()

![IMG-59: Picture of a wheelchair]()

**Each type provides a different level of support and has multiple variations designed to accommodate a wide range of body sizes and needs.**
---
### Choosing the Right Assistive Device

**Choosing the right assistive device is imperative to minimize fall risk. Follow this two-step plan to determine which assistive device is best for you:**

**Step 1: Start by identifying the appropriate assistive device type.**

- Canes: Suitable for people with mild balance issues.
- 4 wheel rolling walkers: Ideal for people with mild to moderate balance issues or low endurance.
- 2 wheel rolling walkers: Best for people with moderate + to significant balance challenges.
- Wheelchairs: Designed for people with major balance deficits.

**Step 2: If necessary, select a variation from the standard assistive device model that accommodates for any specific body characteristic or use case need.**

- Junior size: For shorter individuals.
- Tall size: For taller individuals.
- Bariatric size: For those with higher weight.
- Lightweight: For frequent travelers.
- Super Light: For frequent travelers with limited strength.
- Large-wheel: For rough terrain or smoother ride.

**For a detailed description of each assistive device and instructions on ordering, please refer to the Appendix of Assistive Devices.**

products mentioned could have a link to the Appendix Section for ordering.

### Fitting an Assistive Device

**Properly fitting an assistive device is essential to maximizing safety and efficiency with use. Follow this two-step process To properly fit a cane or rolling walker.**

- Stand in your normal posture with arms hanging at your side.
- Adjust the height of the cane or walker handle at or just above the wrist.

modules.title: Posture
modules.subtitle: Step 8
modules.body:
**The eighth step in the Fall Prevention Plan is maintaining good posture.**
---
![IMG-61: Picture of someone standing with good posture.]()

**Posture, or how you hold your body, is key to having good balance.**
---
![IMG-62: Picture of someone with bad posture]()

**Unfortunately, posture will often deteriorate with age**, **and can, if left unaddressed, lead to increased fall risk.** The most common posture changes seen in older adults include a forward, backward, and/or lateral leaning trunk, rounded upper back, protruding neck and head, and bent knees
---

### To improve posture and reduce fall risk, focus on these strategies:

1. Stand tall with an upright trunk, shoulders and head back, and knees straight.
2. While walking, fix your gaze twenty to thirty feet ahead of body, not on the ground right in front of you, unless navigating a known trip hazard.
3. Take steps that extend in front of the body, landing heel-first.
4. Perform postural stretches 2-3 times per week.

**Watch this video to improve posture and reduce fall risk.**

[video:V3 Link to video showing an upright posture, appropriate walking technique and postural stretch.]()

modules.title: Strength Training for Fall Prevention
modules.subtitle: Step 9
modules.body:
**The ninth step in the Fall Prevention Plan is to be physically strong.**
---
![IMG-64: Picture of an older person hiking on a mountain top with a majestic setting.]()

**Strength is critical for preventing falls.** It forms the foundation for good balance and is directly correlated to fall risk. Maintaining strength through the aging process however is not a given, it requires effort, and without regular performance of activities that build strength, muscles will weaken over time, and fall risk will increase.
---
![IMG-65: Picture of an older adult working out in the gym.]()

**Performing Strengthening Exercises is the solution.** They build muscle, lower fall risk, and are therefore a key component of a successful Fall Prevention Plan. Fortunately, strengthening exercise programs designed to reduce falls don't have to be elaborate to be effective. Research shows that regular performance of even a few targeted exercises, done to a point of fatigue can build muscle and significantly reduce fall risk.
---
![IMG-66: Picture of an older adult working out at home.]()

**Exercises can be done at home or in a gym, and can even be selected to match your time availability and overall interest level.** The key to success with an exercise program is choosing a routine that you'll stick with. It is best to start with a small program, and gradually add more exercises if desired, versus jumping into a large program and possibly quitting before exercise benefits are realized.
---
**To reduce fall risk, find a balance focused exercise program that works for you and stick to it!**
---
### Selecting the Appropriate Exercise Program

**Presented below are 3 Home Exercise Programs and 1 Fitness Center Program specifically designed for fall prevention.** They are listed in order of increasing complexity and time required to complete them.  Each program has sections that address strength, flexibility, and endurance, and instructions are provided in how to correctly perform each one. Review the programs and **select the one that most closely matches your commitment level and time availability.**
---
### Exercise Programs for Fall Prevention

### Level 1 Home Exercise Program for Fall Prevention

- Time Commitment = Low
- Complexity = Low

[video:V4 Level 1 Home Exercise Program for Fall Prevention Video Link]()

### Written Instructions

### Level 1 Home Exercise Program for Fall Prevention

**Strength:** perform 2–3 times per week.

- Heel ups: stand with your feet at shoulder width apart and holding a firm surface for support. Rise up on your toes as high as able, then relax and return to the original position. Repeat to muscle fatigue.
- Sit-to-stand: sit on a regular height chair that has a firm seat. Stand to an upright position, then relax and return to the seated position. Use your hands only if needed. Repeat to muscle fatigue.

**Flexibility:** perform 2–3 times per week.

- Chest Stretch: sit towards the front of a chair with your head and trunk erect, and your hands clasped behind your back. Pull your shoulders back until a "strong, but comfortable" stretch is felt across the chest. Hold 15 seconds. Perform 2-3 times. This stretch can also be performed in standing, if your balance status allows.

**Endurance:** perform 3–5 times per week.

- Walk on flat indoor or outdoor terrain, using a cane or walker as necessary, targeting a 20–30 minute duration at a moderate intensity, and stopping if needed. Do not use a treadmill. If walking is too difficult, see option 2 below.

modules.body:
**The final, and arguably, most important step in the Fall Prevention Plan is to maximize balance.**
---
![IMG-70: Picture of older person engaged in an activity that involves balance, e.g. older person jumping between rocks in a stream or playing a sport]()

**Balance, or the act of maintaining a steady position, is the body's primary defense against falling.** Unfortunately, unless a person is actively engaged in activities that preserve it, balance, like strength, will deteriorate with age and fall risk will increase
---

![IMG-71: Picture of older person doing balance exercises]()

**Fortunately, there is hope, balance can be maintained and improved.** Research shows that consistent performance of even a limited number of balance exercises increases body stability and lowers fall risk, and that well-designed balance programs are the gold standard in fall prevention due to their effectiveness in improving balance, safety confidence, and fall avoidance.
---
**If you are serious about reducing fall risk, performing a well-designed balance program is strongly recommended.**
---
### Selecting the Appropriate Balance Program

**Presented below are six balance programs specifically designed to reduce the risk of falls.**

They are listed in order of increasing intensity and are labeled to indicate the fall risk level they are designed to target. Review each of the programs and select the one that most closely matches your current balance and fall risk level. As your balance improves, progress to the next Balance Program Level.

**An important note: each program is preceded by specific safety instructions to be used during their performance. Please follow the provided safety strategies recommended for each program.**

modules.title: If a Fall Occurs
modules.subtitle: Chapter 3
modules.body:
**Falls are typically sudden and startling events that often leave the faller stunned and scared. Unfortunately, even with careful planning and attention to safety, falls can still happen.**

![IMG-78: Picture of a stunned, overwhelmed older adult; person can be on the floor alone or with a family member; looking to be in a state of bewilderment, trying to assess their situation.]()

**Since preventing every fall is impossible, knowing how to reduce fall related injury risk, react immediately after a fall occurs, stand up safely from the ground, and manage any post fall fears is important.** The following guidelines outline the best strategies to handle each of these problems.

modules.title: Minimizing the Risk of a Fall-Related Injury
modules.subtitle: Section 1
modules.body:
![IMG-79: Picture of a hospital]()

**CDC statistics reveal** that 37% of falls result in an injury that limits activity for at least one day and 20% of falls result in an injury that requires hospitalization.
---
![IMG-80: Picture of a nursing home]()

**Knowing how to minimize the risk of a fall related injury is therefore critical** as it could mean the difference between a minor injury or bruised ego and a serious injury that requires surgery or even nursing home placement.

**Reducing the risk of a fall related injury needs to be considered from both short term and long-term perspectives. Here are the strategies recommended to reduce the risk of both types of fall related injuries:**

**Reducing the risk of a fall related injury from a long-term perspective focuses on building stronger bones. To do this, follow these tips:**

- Get adequate calcium and vitamin D. Guidelines set forth by the Mayo Clinic recommends that Senior adults get 1200 milligram calcium and 800 - 1000 IU Vitamin D daily per day.
- Stay active, getting at least one hundred fifty minutes of exercise weekly.
- Quit smoking.
- Limit alcohol consumption.
- Maintain a healthy body weight.
- Talk to your doctor about osteoporosis.

**Reducing the immediate risk of a fall related injury involves knowing how to fall. To do this, use these tips:**

**If you feel yourself beginning to fall...**

- Steer your body away from hard furniture, sharp objects, or hard floors.
- Aim to land on softer body parts, like your bottom.
- Instead of using your arms to break the fall, turn your body and shield your head with your arms.
- Relax your body as you fall, going limp and rolling naturally upon impact with the ground.

[video:V13 Video Demonstrating How to Fall]()

![IMG-82: Picture of older person lying on the ground after a fall; person is calm/in control of situation and possibly checking for injury.]()

### How to React Immediately After a Fall

**Responding appropriately to a fall is vital.** It reduces the risk of a sustained injury worsening, improves recovery chances, and reduces long-term damage risk.

### If you fall, follow these steps:

- Stay calm, take deep breaths, and check for injuries.
- If possible, slide or crawl to a nearby chair or couch to help you stand.
- If seriously injured, don't try to stand; call for help instead.
- If you can't get up or are seriously injured, crawl or slide to a phone and call 911.

modules.title: Standing Up from the Ground After a Fall
modules.subtitle: Section 2
modules.body:
![IMG-83: Picture of older person trying to stand up from the ground.]()

**Standing up from the ground can be challenging for older adults, especially after a fall**. There are two proven methods to get up, the Crawling Method and the Lifting Yourself Onto A Low Surface Method

### Using the “Crawling Method” to Stand Up from the Ground

- Roll onto your side.
- Push up onto your hands and knees into a crawling position.
- Crawl to a sturdy chair, coffee table, or couch.
- Place your hands on the furniture, extend your stronger leg, and push into a half-lunge to stand.
- If standing fully is difficult, turn and sit on the furniture. If knee pain prevents crawling, scoot on your bottom or roll to the furniture.

[video:V14 Video demonstration of Crawling Method to get up from the floor.]()
---
**Using the “Lifting Yourself onto a Low Surface” Method to Stand Up from the Ground**

- Scoot close to a staircase, coffee table, chair, or sofa.
- Push into a seated position using your hands on the floor.
- Turn so your back faces the furniture.
- Lift your bottom onto the surface. If using a staircase, sit on the lowest step and move up step by step until you can stand.

[video:V15 Video demonstration of Using a Nearby Surface to get up from the floor.]()

modules.title: Overcoming the Fear of Falling
modules.subtitle: Section 3
modules.body:
![IMG-86: Picture of an older adult looking somewhat fearful or hesitant of walking 87]()

**The fear of falling is a very serious, but often overlooked problem for senior adults.** It affects over 50% of people who have fallen in the past and more than 30% of the general senior adult population.
---
![IMG-87: Picture of a depressed/socially isolated older adult]()

**If unaddressed, the fear of falling can lead to** decreased participation in normal daily activity, social isolation, depression, physical decline, and ultimately increased fall risk.
---

### To overcome the fear of falling, follow these steps:

- Discuss the problem with your physician and/or those closest to you to determine any obvious cause.
- Remove or discontinue anything that may be causing a fear of falling.
- Resume activity as quickly as possible, starting with safe activities to build confidence if needed and then gradually increasing their intensity as you are able.

modules.title: When Falls are a Warning Sign of an Underlying Health Problem
modules.subtitle: Section 4
modules.body:
![IMG-88: Picture of a warning sign]()

**Impaired balance and falling can actually be a warning sign of an underlying health issue.**
---
![IMG-89: Picture of a older adult speaking to a doctor.]()

**If falls occur in the presence of other physical conditions** such as persistent pain, swelling, shortness of breath, lethargy, or dizziness, a medical evaluation should be performed.
---
**Pain** can signal tissue injury or joint damage; **Dizziness** can be due to dehydration, adverse medication side effects, vestibular system disorders or extremes in blood pressure and sugar levels; **Swelling** can be a result of tissue injury or problems with the heart, kidney, and lymphatic systems; **Lethargy** is often caused by infection or electrolyte imbalance; and **Shortness of Breath** can be a result of heart or lung problems. If balance problems or falls appear to be associated with a physical condition such as persistent pain, swelling, shortness of breath, lethargy or dizziness, a medical assessment is strongly recommended to rule out an underlying health problem.

modules.title: Home Safety Equipment and Modification Appendix
modules.subtitle: Chapter 5
modules.body:
**Maximizing the safety of the home environment is one of the best strategies to prevent falls, however knowing which products would be the most beneficial can be confusing.**

![IMG-113: Picture of a raised toilet seat]()

![IMG-117: Picture of a mechanical stair lift]()

![IMG-116: Picture of a elevating chair]()

![IMG-115: Picture of a shower chair]()

![IMG-114: Picture of a tub bench]()

**This section provides a room-by-room outline and description of the most common products and methods used to decrease the risk of falls in the home.** Pictures of each piece of equipment are given and instructions and discount code for ordering from Amazon are provided.

modules.title: The Bathroom
modules.subtitle: Section 1
modules.body:
![IMG-118: Picture of a slip resistant rug/mat]()

- Place a **Slip Resistant Rug or Mat** next to the bathtub/shower when bathing for improved safety during entry and exit.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0alvBwRp)

![IMG-119: Picture of Non Skid Strips]()

- Use **Non-Skid Strips** or a **Bath Mat** on the bathtub/shower floor to prevent slipping while bathing.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0d9xWkRZ)

![IMG-120: Picture of Bath Mat]()

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0fjlndpN)

![IMG-121: Picture of Grab Bars]()

- Install **Grab Bars** in and around the bathtub/shower for improved standing balance.

Special Note: Grab bars should be mounted at a height just above waist level and in such a way that creates an almost continuous support surface starting outside the bathtub/shower and continuing throughout the entire bathing area. Towel racks and suction cup style grab bars should not be considered an adequate replacement for properly mounted grab bars.

![IMG-122: Diagram of Shower Area with Position of Grab Bars shown]()

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/07qqw31i)

![IMG-123: picture of shower chair with back and arms.]()

- Use a **Shower Chair with Back and Arms** in the bathtub/shower if standing balance or endurance is significantly compromised.

Special Feature: A shower chair with back and arms provides a safe sitting surface to perform bathing needs, is easy to stand up and down from, and when used in combination with grab bars, creates a very safe bathing area.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/008u5Gxx)

![IMG-124: Picture of a Tub Bench]()

- Use a **Tub Bench** if stepping over the bathtub wall or shower is unsafe.

Special Note: To use, the bather sits down on the Tub Bench outside of the bathtub/shower, then scoots across the bench into the bathing area.

![IMG-125: Picture of a Modified Shower Curtain]()

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/01uC1RpB)

A **Modified Shower Curtain** can be used to limit the amount of water that escapes the bathing area.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/02eyVte7)

![IMG-126: Picture of a Tub Bench with a Sliding and Pivoting seat.]()

- A variation to the basic tub bench is the **Tub Bench with a Sliding and Pivoting Seat**.

Special Feature: This piece of equipment is used if the bather is not strong enough to scoot across the elongated Tub Bench seat into the bathtub/shower or does not possess adequate postural control to sit unsupported when scooting or bathing. To use, the bather sits down on the Tub Bench Seat outside of the bathing area, buckles in, pivots the chair direction and then slides into the bathing area on the tub bench seat.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0deJQVQl)

- Use a **Modified Toilet Seat** if standing up or down from a toilet is difficult or unsafe. There are multiple designs available, each with their own specific use case. Let's consider the most common designs below:

![IMG-127: Picture of Versa Frame]()

- **Versa Frame**: adds arms to a toilet thereby providing a stable surface to grasp when sitting down and to push up from when sitting. This product is recommended when the toilet height is adequate, but use of arms is needed to sit or stand safely.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0cgRcoED)

![IMG-128: Picture of a Raised Toilet Seat w/arms.]()

- **Raised Toilet Seat with Arms:** adds arms and extra height to toilet; used when toilet is too low and use of arms is needed to stand.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/03ubjpRV)

- **Three in One Commode:**

![IMG-129: Picture of a Raised Toilet Seat w/arms]()

Special Feature: provides arms to assist with standing up or sitting down, has an adjustable toilet seat height, is portable, and certain designs are more accommodating to larger people. Used when existing toilet is too low, use of arms are needed to safely stand or sit, other modified toilet seats are two confining, and/or the unit needs to be used in multiple locations or for multiple purposes (at bedside for nighttime toileting needs or in the shower/bathtub as a shower chair).

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0hMYMIIM)

modules.title: The Bedroom
modules.subtitle: Section 2
modules.body:
- **Create a designated dressing area in the bedroom or bathroom**. Furnish the area with a heavy chair with arms to sit on and a solid surface to hold onto when standing.
---

- **Adjust Bed height to maximize safety**. Beds that are either too tall or too short make trying to get in or out of bed difficult and dangerous. Optimum bed heights range between 18 --> 23 inches when the mattress is sat on by an average height male or female.

![IMG-130: Picture of a reduced height Box Spring]()

Beds can be lowered by replacing the traditional box spring with a **Reduced Height Box Spring**. Multiple heights are available and should be selected to accommodate a person's individual need.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0eO8x7fV)

Beds can be raised by using **Furniture Risers**. Multiple heights of this product are also available and should be selected to accommodate a person's individual need.

Special Note: If using furniture risers, make sure the inside base of riser is large enough to accommodate the foot of the bed frame.  Using a stool to get in and out of a tall bed, even if it has a built-in handrail, is not recommended.

![IMG-131: Picture of Furniture Riser]()

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/05Dku18o)

![IMG-132: Picture of  a Bed Rail]()

- Use a **Bed Rail** if getting in/out of bed is difficult or if safety during sitting or standing at the bed is compromised. Bed Rails secure to the bed frame or under the mattress and provided an easy to grasp support surface for the balance compromised person.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0gJXxjca)
---
![IMG-133: Picture of a Wonder Pole]()

- A **Wonder Pole** is a good alternative to a bed rail.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/07IG3EPp)

![IMG-134: Picture of  a stair handrail.]()

modules.title: The Living Room/Den
modules.subtitle: Section 4
modules.body:
![IMG-137: Picture of  furniture riser]()

- Use **Furniture Risers** to elevate chairs and couches that are low and difficult to stand up from.

Special Note: Optimum sitting surface height is 18–22 inches when surface is sat on. This height range maximizes the combination of sitting comfort and ease of standing. Furniture Riser come in multiple heights and should be selected to accommodate a person's individual need.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/05Dku18o)

![IMG-138: Picture of  a recliner chair base.]()

- Use a **Recliner Chair Riser Base** to increase the height of a recliner chair if standing up/down is difficult.

[Buy on Amazon](https://a.co/d/0ehAz0jn)

![IMG-139: Picture of  an elevating recliner chair.]()

- Use **an Elevating Recliner Chair** if standing up/down requires assistance. Elevating recliner chairs should only be used if standing up is markedly difficult or unsafe. For people with poor sitting balance, and/or trunk control choose a non-slick covering material such as a knit fabric to minimize the risk of sliding out of chair when chair is in raised position. Rest is required.

Amazon Link to Elevating Recliner Chair:   <https://www.la-z-boy.com/b/living-room/recliners/power-lift-chairs>

modules.title: Summing It Up
modules.subtitle: Chapter 6
modules.body:
![IMG-140: Picture of older couple walking with canes; happy, hopeful]()

**Falls are far too common** among older adults, and their consequences—physical injury, loss of independence, fear, diminished quality of life, and even death—can be devastating. **Fortunately, the evidence is clear: falls don't have to be an inevitable part of aging. Most falls can be prevented** through awareness, assessment, a targeted plan, and consistent follow through.

**In the Fall Prevention Plan, you have learned the full scope of the problem**, how to accurately quantify your personal fall risk, identify the specific factors most likely causing your unsteadiness, and respond effectively if a fall does occur. **Most importantly, you have gained an effective 10-Point Strategy to reduce your risk of falls:**

•  Developing a safety-first **mindset**

•  Choosing stable, supportive **footwear**

•  Maintaining clear **vision**

•  Managing **medications** for safety

•  Prioritizing proper **nutrition and hydration**

•  Improving **posture** and body mechanics

•  Creating a **safe home environment**

•  Selecting the right **assistive devices**

•  Building **strength**

•  Enhancing **balance**

![IMG-141: Picture of older people smiling, laughing with family, grandchildren.]()

These steps aren't meant to be isolated tips— each one plays an integral role in a complete plan, that when working together, creates a powerful protection from falls. **Here's the good news —> you now hold the power to dramatically reduce your risk of falls. Seniors who have implemented these strategies have regained confidence, stayed active longer, and continued to enjoy the independence they value**; and you can too. Start with the areas that feel most relevant to you, track your progress, reassess your fall risk periodically, and continue building out until the full program is in place.

**You deserve to live safely, move freely, and less fearful of falling. By committing to the Fall Prevention Plan today, you're taking a meaningful step toward a stronger, steadier, and more secure tomorrow. Stay committed to a fall free life, stay focused, and never give up!**
